```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# Every chunk below is eval = FALSE: authoring or deploying a private template
# needs a git server, a private package, or a writable cache directory, none
# of which exist at `R CMD check` time.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

## Why private templates

The `dta-template.yaml` files packaged in `inst/extdata/templates` — including
`biomarker_gf.dta-template.yaml` — are worked *examples*. They ship in an
open-source repository, which means anyone who installs DTAtools can read
them. A real Data Transfer Specification names a real supplier, a real
receiving organisation, and real contact people. That content must never live
in a public package, and it must never be one accidental commit away from
being in one either.

The template engine behind `run_dta_app()`'s "Create new from template"
picker therefore does not require its templates to live inside DTAtools at
all. It can instead load them from a private git repository, an internal R
package, or a local directory that is never checked into this repository —
configured entirely through environment variables, so a Posit Connect
deployment can point at your organisation's own template family without a
single code change.

## Deploying on Posit Connect

The headline feature is one content environment variable. Setting it is
enough to switch the app from the packaged examples to your own private
template family:

```r
DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_SOURCES = "acme=git:https://bitbucket.example.com/scm/proj/dta-templates.git#main"
```

The full variable reference, with the defaults the code actually falls back
to when a variable is unset:

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_SOURCES` | `""` (none configured) | `"[name=]scheme:locator[#ref]; ..."` — one or more sources, `;`-separated. See "The three source schemes" below. |
| `DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_INCLUDE_BUILTIN` | unset (reads as `FALSE` once a private source is configured) | Set to `1`, `true`, or `yes` to keep the packaged/legacy template directories available *alongside* a configured private source. Meaningless — always effectively `TRUE` — when no private source is configured at all. |
| `DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_REFRESH_SECONDS` | `900` | How long a cached `git:` checkout (and the in-process template index built from it) is trusted before it is re-fetched/rebuilt. An unparseable or non-positive value is ignored with a warning, falling back to `900`. |
| `DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_CACHE_DIR` | unset — falls back to `tools::R_user_dir("DTAtools", "cache")`, and if that is not writable (common on a Connect content sandbox), to a directory under `tempdir()` | Where `git:` clones are cached. |
| `DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_GIT_TOKEN` | unset (anonymous clone) | Credential for a private `git:` source. Only ever set as a git child-process environment variable — see "The three source schemes" below for why. |
| `DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_GIT_USER` | `"git"` | Basic-auth username sent alongside `DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_GIT_TOKEN` when `DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_GIT_AUTH` is `"basic"`. |
| `DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_GIT_AUTH` | `"basic"` | `"basic"` or `"bearer"` — which kind of `Authorization` header the token becomes. |

Three behaviours are deliberate and worth knowing before you flip the switch:

- **Setting `DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_SOURCES` switches the app to private-only.**
  The packaged/legacy directories (the `biomarker_gf` example among them) are
  dropped from the search path the moment any private source is configured,
  unless you explicitly ask to keep them with
  `DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_INCLUDE_BUILTIN=1`. An internal deployment that ships a
  real template family must not let a failed private source silently fall
  back to the demo — someone would eventually author a genuine specification
  from an example template without ever finding out the real source was
  unreachable.
- **A failed source serves its last-good cache, with a staleness warning.**
  If a `git:` refresh fails (network blip, expired token, unreachable host)
  but a previous checkout already exists on disk, the app keeps using that
  checkout rather than breaking template creation outright. The failure is
  still surfaced — the resolved source is flagged stale, with the age of the
  cache and the underlying git error attached.
- **A cold start with no cache offers NO templates — never the packaged
  examples.** If a `git:` source has never successfully resolved on this
  machine (first deployment, or a cache that was wiped), there is nothing to
  serve, stale or otherwise, and the picker comes up empty rather than
  quietly substituting the demo template. This is the same reasoning as the
  point above, taken to its limit: a private-only deployment has decided the
  packaged example is *never* an acceptable substitute for the real thing, so
  the failure has to be visible, not merely degraded.

## The three source schemes

`DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_SOURCES` is a flat string, not YAML or JSON, because it
lives in a single environment variable set by ops tooling — a Connect "Vars"
field, a Helm chart, a systemd unit file — where a multi-line or quoted value
is an easy way to get silently mangled in transit. The grammar is:

```
[name=]scheme:locator[#ref]; [name=]scheme:locator[#ref]; ...
```

### `dir:` — a local directory

```r
DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_SOURCES = "site=dir:/srv/dta-templates"
```

The locator is a path that must already exist and be readable; `dir:` sources
are resolved with no network or credential involved at all. Useful for a
template family kept on the same host as the app, or mounted into the
container.

### `pkg:` — a companion R package

```r
DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_SOURCES = "acme=pkg:acme.dta.templates"
```

The locator is an R package name. It must be installed and expose an
`inst/dta-templates` directory (i.e. `system.file("dta-templates", package =
"acme.dta.templates")` must resolve). This is the right shape when your
templates are versioned and released the same way any other internal R
package is.

### `git:` — a private git repository

```r
DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_SOURCES = "acme=git:https://bitbucket.example.com/scm/proj/dta-templates.git#main"
```

The scheme is always the first token up to the first `:` — this matters here
specifically because the locator is itself a URL containing `://`. `git:
https://host/x.git` parses to scheme `git` and locator `https://host/x.git`,
not a second split on the colon inside `https://`. The optional `#ref` names
a branch or tag to shallow-clone (`--depth 1`); omitted, it defaults to
`HEAD`.

Both **Bitbucket Data Center** (production, in this deployment's case) and
**GitHub** (used to mirror the same repository for CI) are reached the same
way — plain HTTPS, credential in `DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_GIT_TOKEN`:

```r
# Bitbucket Data Center HTTP access token, sent as HTTP Basic auth
DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_SOURCES = "acme=git:https://bitbucket.example.com/scm/proj/dta-templates.git#main"
DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_GIT_TOKEN = "<bitbucket-http-access-token>"
DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_GIT_AUTH  = "basic"    # the default; shown for clarity

# GitHub, same repository mirrored for CI, PAT sent as a bearer token
DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_SOURCES = "acme=git:https://github.com/example-org/dta-templates.git#main"
DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_GIT_TOKEN = "<github-pat>"
DTATOOLS_TEMPLATE_GIT_AUTH  = "bearer"
```

**The token never reaches the command line, a URL, or disk.** It is passed to
the `git` child process purely as an environment variable
(`GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0`/`GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0`, delivering an `http.extraHeader`),
never embedded in the clone URL and never passed as a `-c` command-line flag.
An `https://user:TOKEN@host/repo.git`-style URL would persist the token in
`.git/config` forever, readable by anyone who later runs `git remote -v`; a
command-line argument is visible to every other user on the machine via the
process table. The environment block of a child process is legible only to
that process's own owner, which is why that is the only place the token ever
lives — and only for the duration of the one `git` call that needs it; the
app's own process environment is restored immediately afterwards.

## Authoring a creation template

A creation template (`kind: dta_creation_template`) builds a whole new DTA.
Here is the real, complete `biomarker_gf.dta-template.yaml` header and one
representative option, trimmed for length:

```yaml
kind: dta_creation_template
id: biomarker_gf
label: Biomarker GF DTS
version: "1.0"
description: >-
  Creates a new DTA for Biomarker GF transfer specifications using the
  bundled GF dataset structure, then applies option-driven metadata fields.

base:
  metadata:
    title: BIOMARKER GF DATA TRANSFER SPECIFICATIONS (DTS)
    version: "1.0"
    date: "${today}"
    header: Test Company 1
    version_history:
      - version: "${version}"
        date: "${today}"
        changes: Initial template-generated version
    receiver:
      affiliation:
        name: Our company
      contacts: []
    supplier:
      affiliation:
        name: External Supplier
      contacts: []
    transmission:
      type: Secure EDT server (SSH sFTP)
      frequency: one-time
      notification: email
      test_upload: true
      blinded_transfer: true
      date_first_transfer: 3 weeks after first batch of sample delivery
      date_last_transfer: 2 weeks after last batch of samples arrive at laboratory
    error_handling: >-
      Format or content errors are reported by email to the authorized
      contacts and corrected in a follow-up transfer.
    authorized_for_corrections: TDM

options:
  - id: title
    label: Document title
    type: text
    target: metadata.title
    help: Title shown on the DTS document. Pick a suggestion or type your own.
    choices:
      - BIOMARKER GF DATA TRANSFER SPECIFICATIONS (DTS)
      - GENOMIC FINDINGS (GF) DATA TRANSFER SPECIFICATIONS

datasets:
  - template: gf_smrnaseq@3.0
    as: gf_data_specs_pattern

party_slots:
  - id: supplier
    label: Supplier
    target: metadata.supplier
  - id: receiver
    label: Receiver
    target: metadata.receiver
```

`${today}` and `${version}` are resolved when the DTA is actually created, so
a document made from this template is dated the day it was made, and its
first `version_history` entry always agrees with the version the user chose
for it. Every `target:` on an option must resolve to a real `DTAMetaData`
field — `base.metadata`'s own keys are validated the same way, so a typo'd
field name aborts template creation immediately rather than silently being
dropped.

## Reusable dataset templates

A creation template does not have to inline its dataset structure. The
`datasets:` entry above, `{template: gf_smrnaseq@3.0, as: gf_data_specs_pattern}`,
imports a **dataset template** (`kind: dta_dataset_template`) instead — a
standalone, reusable column/rule set that can be shared across several
creation templates, or dropped into an existing DTA as a second dataset. Here
is the real header and a representative column from
`gf_smrnaseq.dta-dataset-template.yaml`:

```yaml
kind: dta_dataset_template
id: gf_smrnaseq
version: "3.0"
label: GF domain smrnaseq
description: Genomic Findings data table with pattern for filename
date: 2024-12-17

options:
  - id: vendor_name
    label: Vendor name
    type: text
    target: dataset.columns.GFNAM.values
    default: ExternalSupplierName
    help: Name or identifier of the data supplier who provides the test results.

dataset:
  name: gf_data_specs_pattern
  type: tabular
  files:
    filename: gf_data_small_smirna.tsv
    type: tsv
  columns:
    - id: GFNAM
      label: Vendor Name
      type: SAS Char
      format: SAS $60.
      nullable: No
      description: Name or identifier of the data supplier who provides the test results.
      values:
        - ExternalSupplierName
  rules: []
```

The `{template:, as:, options:, patch:}` shape a creation template's
`datasets:` entry uses to import one of these:

- `template:` — the `id@version` (or bare `id`) of the dataset template.
- `as:` — rename the built dataset, so the same dataset template can be
  imported twice into one DTA under two different names.
- `options:` — selections for the dataset template's own `options:` (here,
  `vendor_name`); anything not selected falls back to that option's
  `default:`.
- `patch:` — free-form column add/remove/modify plus general field sets, for
  a deviation that does not warrant its own dataset-template version.

A patch's four operations always run in this fixed order, and the order is
load-bearing, not incidental:

1. **`remove_columns`** — shrink first, so a column marked for removal is
   already gone before anything below tries to address it.
2. **`add_columns`** — grow second, so a new column exists before
   `modify_columns` or `set` could otherwise address it by id.
3. **`modify_columns`** — adjust existing columns third, once the column
   list has its final membership (the right ids present, the wrong ones
   already removed).
4. **`set`** — general dotted-path field sets last, so a `set:` path against
   `columns.<id>.<field>` always resolves against the *final* column list,
   never an id an earlier step in the same patch was still going to
   invalidate.

That ordering is what lets one patch remove a column, add a differently-named
replacement, tweak an unrelated existing column, and set a top-level field —
all in the same block — without the steps fighting over which column exists
yet.

## Deviation templates

A supplier-specific deviation does not need to restate a whole template family
just to change a handful of fields. `biomarker_gf_acme.dta-template.yaml`, in
full, `extends:` the base template above:

```yaml
kind: dta_creation_template
id: biomarker_gf_acme
label: Biomarker GF DTS (ACME Labs)
version: "1.0"
extends: biomarker_gf@1.0
description: >-
  ACME Labs supplier deviation of biomarker_gf: names ACME as the vendor,
  clarifies GFNAM for ACME, and adds ACME's own internal sample identifier
  column. Everything else -- base metadata, the other 11 options, the party
  slots -- is inherited unchanged from the parent.

options:
  - id: header
    default: ACME Labs

datasets:
  - template: gf_smrnaseq@3.0
    as: gf_data_specs_pattern
    options:
      vendor_name: ACME Labs
    patch:
      modify_columns:
        - id: GFNAM
          description: Name of the ACME sequencing facility supplying the results.
      add_columns:
        - id: ACMEID
          label: ACME internal identifier
          type: SAS Char
          format: SAS $20.
          nullable: Yes
          description: ACME's internal sample identifier, for query resolution.
```

The merge is a recursive deep merge, child over parent:

- A mapping key present in both parent and child merges recursively; a
  sequence, scalar, or a mapping paired with a non-mapping parent is a
  wholesale replacement (merging a list of column specs by position would
  silently splice unrelated columns together the moment the child's list is a
  different length).
- `options:` and `party_slots:` entries are matched and merged **by `id`**,
  keeping the parent's position for an inherited entry; a child option can
  carry `remove: true` to drop an inherited one entirely.
- `datasets:` entries are matched by identity — `as:`, else `template:` (with
  any `@version` pin stripped, so `gf@3.0` and `gf@4.0` still name the same
  slot), else `source:`, else `name:` — so a deviation's `patch:` merges into
  the *same* dataset entry the parent declared, rather than appending a
  second, unrelated one.
- **An explicit `null` in the child removes an inherited key.** `key: ~` or
  `key: null` in a child mapping is not "leave this at whatever the parent
  set" (that is what *omitting* the key means) — it is an instruction to
  delete it from the merged result.

`biomarker_gf_acme` above omits `base:` entirely, and that is deliberate and
supported: a child that `extends:` another template inherits the parent's
`base:` (and, by the same rule, its `datasets:`) verbatim when it states
nothing of its own. **`base: {}` is not the same thing.** An *absent* `base:`
leaves the parent's section completely untouched; an explicitly empty mapping
is a real instruction — "replace `base:` with nothing" — and wipes out every
field the parent set. Absent and empty are deliberately kept distinguishable
for exactly this reason; write `base:` at all only when you mean to override
part of it.

## Versioning

Every template — creation, dataset, or party profile — declares its own
`id` and `version`, and a reference to one is written `id@version`, or a bare
`id` (equivalently, `id@latest`) to mean "the newest version available":

```r
# in a `datasets:` entry, an `extends:`, or a rebase target
"gf_smrnaseq@3.0"     # exact version 3.0
"biomarker_gf"        # newest version of biomarker_gf, whatever that is today
"biomarker_gf@latest" # same as above, written explicitly
```

### Pinning versus following

A deviation template usually wants to **follow** the standard it deviates from,
so that publishing a new version of the standard does not mean editing every
supplier's file to pick it up. Write `extends: biomarker_gf@latest`, and the
shipped `biomarker_gf_acme.dta-template.yaml` does exactly that:

```yaml
# follows the current standard; no edit needed when biomarker_gf is republished
extends: biomarker_gf@latest
```

This does **not** make finished documents drift. Creation resolves `@latest`
once and records the concrete version it chose in `metadata.template`, so a
specification that was built from `biomarker_gf@1.0` still says so after `1.1`
is published, and rebasing it later still reconstructs the right ancestor. Only
*new* documents follow the parent forward.

Pin an exact version instead when a deviation has been agreed against one
specific release of the standard and must not move until it is re-agreed:

```yaml
extends: biomarker_gf@1.0
```

The same choice applies to a `datasets:` import. There the default leans the
other way: a `patch:` names specific columns, so it is only known to be
coherent against a dataset template whose column set it has actually been
checked against. The shipped ACME example therefore follows the *document*
standard with `@latest` but pins the *dataset* template it patches:

```yaml
datasets:
  - template: gf_smrnaseq@3.0     # pinned: the patch below names its columns
    as: gf_data_specs_pattern
    patch:
      add_columns:
        - { id: ACMEID, label: ACME internal identifier, type: SAS Char }
```

Whichever you choose, `validate_template()` is the safety net: its dry-run
instantiation builds every non-abstract template, so a deviation that
`@latest` has quietly carried onto an incompatible parent fails your private
repository's CI rather than surfacing when someone creates a document.

**Always quote the version:** `version: "1.0"`, never `version: 1.0`. YAML
parses an unquoted `1.10` as the number 1.1 — the trailing zero that
distinguishes "one point ten" from "one point one" simply does not survive an
unquoted numeric scalar, and no code downstream can recover it once that has
happened. `validate_template()` (see "CI for a private template repository"
below) fails an unquoted version outright, with the error code
`version_unquoted` and a message quoting exactly what to write instead — this
is checked at severity `"error"`, not merely `"warning"`, because the failure
mode it prevents is silent and irreversible.

## Parties

A creation template can offer a "party slot" — a dropdown bound to
`metadata.supplier` or `metadata.receiver` — instead of every template author
retyping (or worse, drifting copies of) the same affiliation/contacts block.
`biomarker_gf.dta-template.yaml`'s `party_slots:` (shown above) declares two
slots, one per metadata target; a **party profile** (`kind:
dta_party_profile`) supplies the actual content one of those dropdowns can
pick. Here is the real `supplier_acme.dta-party.yaml` in full:

```yaml
kind: dta_party_profile
id: supplier_acme
version: "1.0"
role: supplier
label: ACME Labs
description: Standard ACME Labs supplier block for the biomarker GF template family.
affiliation:
  name: ACME Labs
  address: 1 Example Way, Springfield
  country: DE
contacts:
  - name: Jane Doe
    role: Data Manager
    email: jane.doe@example.com
    signature: true
  - name: John Roe
    role: Bioinformatics Lead
    email: john.roe@example.com
```

`role:` is `supplier`, `receiver`, or `any`; a slot only ever offers profiles
whose role matches its own target (derived automatically from the target —
`metadata.supplier` implies role `supplier` — unless the slot states its own),
optionally narrowed further by the slot's own `profiles:` allow-list.
Choosing a profile replaces the slot's whole target block (affiliation and
contacts together) — never a partial merge, because merging one profile's
contacts with a different profile's affiliation would silently produce a
document naming the wrong organisation's contact as a signatory for the
other.

**Metadata carry-over** (used when a document is created as a continuation of
an ancestor, e.g. during a version rebase — see the next section) copies a
fixed, *default-on* set of metadata fields from the ancestor unless the caller
states its own list:

```r
c("receiver", "supplier", "transmission", "error_handling",
  "authorized_for_corrections")
```

`title`, `version`, `date`, and `version_history` are *default-off* —
deliberately excluded from that default set. They are the ancestor document's
own identity and revision history, not properties of the supplier/receiver
relationship; a new document must state its own title and start its own
version history rather than impersonating the one it came from.

Carry-over, party slots, and options are applied in a fixed **precedence
order** — `base` metadata, then carry-over, then the chosen party profile,
then option effects — so that anything the current document's own author
actively chooses always wins over whatever an ancestor document happened to
have, and a party-profile choice always wins over a carried-over value at the
same target.

## Controlled vocabularies

A column's permitted values — `values:` — are already enforced: they become a
JSON-Schema `enum`, and validation fails every row that is not one of them.
What was missing was a way to write that list *once* and reuse it. A
**controlled vocabulary** (`kind: dta_vocabulary`, `*.dta-vocabulary.yaml`) is
that list, versioned and indexed like everything else in the family. The
shipped `gf_test.dta-vocabulary.yaml`, in full:

```yaml
kind: dta_vocabulary
id: gf_test
version: "1.0"
label: Genomic measurement tests
type: text            # text | number | integer
terms:
  - code: TRNSCPTN
    label: Transcription
    description: Transcription measurement, reported per reference sequence.
```

A bare string in `terms:` is shorthand for a term with only a `code`.

A vocabulary is **never referenced by a finished document.** It is expanded
into an ordinary `values:` list at creation time, so a DTA YAML you hand to a
supplier is readable without access to your vocabulary library — and nothing
in the validation engine, or in `DTAColumnSpec`, had to learn a new concept.

### Binding a column to one

`values_from:` on a column, in a dataset template or in a creation template's
`patch:`:

```yaml
- id: GFTSTDTL
  type: SAS Char
  values_from: gf_tstdtl@1.0
```

or, spelled out, to restrict the vocabulary for *this* dataset:

```yaml
values_from:
  vocabulary: gf_tstdtl@1.0
  field: code            # code (default) | label
  include: [FRAGMENT COUNT]   # only these terms
  exclude: [NORMALIZED LEVEL] # everything but these
```

An `include:` naming a code the vocabulary does not have is an **error**, not
a silent no-op — that is the exact shape a typo takes, and its only symptom
would be a column whose permitted values quietly omit a term, months later,
against real data.

`field:` is what makes one vocabulary serve a **code/decode pair**, which is
the norm in this domain. The shipped `gf_smrnaseq` dataset template binds both
halves to the same vocabulary, so the two columns cannot drift apart:

```yaml
- id: GFTESTCD
  values_from: {vocabulary: gf_test@1.0, field: code}    # -> TRNSCPTN
- id: GFTEST
  values_from: {vocabulary: gf_test@1.0, field: label}   # -> Transcription
```

### Extending a vocabulary

One vocabulary can build on another. This is *not* the generic `extends:`
merge used elsewhere, and could not be: that merge replaces sequences
wholesale, so "inherit these terms and add one" is not expressible with it.
Extension is explicit:

```yaml
kind: dta_vocabulary
id: visit_oncology
version: "1.0"
extends: visit@1.0
add_terms:
  - { code: C2D1, label: Cycle 2 Day 1 }
remove_terms: [EOT]
```

`add_terms:` naming a code the parent already has **replaces it in place**,
keeping the parent's position — relabelling an inherited term is the common
case and must not reorder the list. A child that states its own `terms:`
replaces the inherited list outright.

### Letting the document's author choose

`values_from:` is the template author's decision. When the choice belongs to
whoever creates the document instead, offer a **vocabulary slot** — the same
shape as a party slot, one concept over. `biomarker_gf.dta-template.yaml`
ships one:

```yaml
vocabulary_slots:
  - id: gf_detail
    label: How are results reported?
    target: datasets.gf_data_specs_pattern.columns.GFTSTDTL.values
    vocabulary: gf_tstdtl@1.0
    mode: closed
    default: [FRAGMENT COUNT, NORMALIZED LEVEL]
    min: 1
```

The "Create new from template" modal renders this as a multi-select of the
vocabulary's terms. `target:` is always
`datasets.<dataset>.columns.<column>.values`; a slot whose target names a
dataset or column the template does not build fails loudly rather than
silently doing nothing.

**`mode:` is about authoring freedom, not looser validation.** `closed` offers
exactly the vocabulary's terms and rejects anything else. `open` additionally
lets the author type a value the vocabulary does not have — "pick from the
vocabulary, or use your own" — and the terms they end up with are *still* a
closed `enum` in the produced document. There is deliberately no "advisory"
mode that would let non-conforming data through: the only way to express that
today is to emit no `values:` at all, which turns the check for that column
completely off, and a check that is silently absent is worse than the problem
it would solve.

### Where a binding may be written

`values_from:` is honoured on a **dataset template's** columns, on columns a
creation template's `patch:` adds or modifies, and on an **inline** dataset
body written directly into a creation template's `datasets:`. It is *not*
honoured in a standalone dataset YAML pulled in with `{source: foo.yaml}` or a
bare `"foo.yaml"` — those files are read as finished specifications, straight
into column objects, with no template pass over them. A `values_from:` written
there fails with a low-level "unused argument" error rather than one of this
feature's own messages. Put the binding in a dataset template instead.

### Two things worth knowing

**Quote nothing, lose nothing — but know why.** Vocabulary files are parsed
with a wider set of YAML scalar handlers than the rest of the template family,
because term codes live in the nastiest corner of YAML 1.1. With an ordinary
parse, `01` and `007` are read as *octal* and become `1` and `7`; `0x1F`
becomes `31`; and `Y`, `N` and `NO` become booleans. Zero-padded visit numbers
and Y/N flags are two of the most common controlled vocabularies there are, so
codes in a `*.dta-vocabulary.yaml` are kept exactly as written, quoted or not.
Coercion to a number happens only when the vocabulary asks for it with
`type: number` or `type: integer`, and a code that cannot be coerced is an
error naming the offending term.

**A new vocabulary version does not reach documents already created.** Creation
expands the terms once and the document owns them from then on — the same
principle as `@latest` for templates (resolve once, record what was chosen,
never drift). Rebase will not move a document onto a newer vocabulary either:
rebase is metadata-only and never touches a dataset's columns. Publishing
`gf_tstdtl@1.1` changes what *new* documents get, and nothing about the old
ones.

## Provenance and upgrading

Every document built from a creation template — through the app, or via
`create_dta_from_template()` with an `index` and a `provenance` argument — gets
a `metadata.template` record: which template `id`/`version` built it, which
source it came from (`source`, `source_kind`, `resolved_commit` for a `git:`
source), the resolved file path, a content hash of the fully `extends:`-merged
definition it was built from, the creation date, its `extends:` lineage, the
`selections` the user actually made, and — for any dataset built from a
dataset template — that dataset's own template provenance.

`metadata.template` is **machine-owned**: it is one of exactly two metadata
fields (`import_issues` is the other) that a template author can never set
from `base.metadata` or an option effect — the allowed-field list used to
validate both is derived from the same set that excludes it. A template
author who could set this field could forge a document's own provenance,
which the rebase feature below would then blindly trust.

**Rebase** moves a document created from template `T@1.0` onto `T@1.1`
without discarding hand edits made since creation. It reconstructs the
document's *ancestor* — what `T@1.0` would have produced with the `selections`
recorded in `metadata.template` — and compares it against both the document
as it stands today and what `T@1.1` would produce with the same selections. A
field that changed only in the target is a template edit; a field that
changed only in the current document is a user edit; a field changed
identically in both is not a conflict; a field changed differently in both is
a conflict requiring an explicit choice.

The limits are worth stating plainly, not glossing over:

- **Metadata only.** Rebase never touches a dataset's columns, rules, or
  files — reconciling those structurally is a substantially different
  problem than merging metadata fields, and is out of scope today. Dataset
  differences are still reported for review; nothing acts on them.
- **`version_history` is never rewritten.** A rebase appends one new entry
  describing the rebase itself; it never edits the document's existing
  history to match the template's own, because that would restate the past
  to match a template the document did not actually come from.
- **A document with no provenance cannot be rebased.** Any document created
  before this feature existed — or created without going through a template
  at all — has no `metadata.template` record and therefore no ancestor to
  reconstruct. Rebasing such a document fails immediately, naming exactly
  that reason, rather than guessing at what it might have come from.

## CI for a private template repository

`validate_template(path, strict = TRUE)` runs the same structural checks the
app's own "Create new from template" picker relies on — an unresolvable
`extends:`, an option `target:` that does not resolve to a real metadata
field (or, worse, one that names a machine-owned field like
`metadata.template`), a party slot naming a profile id that does not exist, a
dataset patch naming an absent column, an unquoted `version:`, a vocabulary
that will not read or whose `extends:` chain cycles, a `values_from:` naming a
vocabulary that is not there or an `include:` code that is not in it — and, as a
final and most comprehensive check, actually builds a DTA from every
non-abstract creation template using its own default selections. `path` may
be a single file or a directory, scanned non-recursively for
`*.dta-template.yaml`, `*.dta-dataset-template.yaml`, `*.dta-party.yaml`, and
`*.dta-vocabulary.yaml` (and their `.yml` spellings).

```r
DTAtools::validate_template(".", strict = TRUE)
```

With `strict = TRUE`, `validate_template()` raises a single error naming every
row of severity `"error"` and stays silent when there are none — the one line
a CI job needs. Without it, the function returns a data frame (`file`, `kind`,
`id`, `version`, `severity`, `code`, `message`) with one row per issue found,
for a human to inspect interactively.

A ready-to-copy GitHub Actions workflow — checkout, install DTAtools from your
internal package source, run the check above — ships at
`system.file("extdata", "templates", "validate-templates.yml", package =
"DTAtools")`. Copy it to `.github/workflows/validate-templates.yml` in the
repository that holds your own templates and fill in the one placeholder step
that installs DTAtools from wherever your organisation hosts it.
